claims.claim: The U.S. Department of Agriculture (Soil Taxonomy, second edition) defines soil as a natural body comprised of solids (minerals and organic matter), liquid, and gases that occurs on the land surface, occupies space, and is characterized by horizons or layers distinguishable from the initial material, or by the ability to support rooted plants in a natural environment; for classification purposes the lower boundary of soil is arbitrarily set at 200 cm.

The five soil-forming factors are climate (including water and temperature effects), macro- and microorganisms, relief (topography), parent material, and time: soil is unconsolidated mineral or organic matter showing the effects of climate and organisms, conditioned by relief, acting on parent material over a period of time.

Soils perform vital functions to sustain plant and animal life, regulate water flow, filter and buffer pollutants, cycle nutrients, and provide physical stability and support; soil is the natural medium for the growth of land plants.

A typical soil is a complex mixture of minerals (approximately 45 percent), organic matter (approximately 5 percent), and empty space (approximately 50 percent, filled to varying degrees with air and water); the mineral content is dominated by clay minerals and quartz, with minor feldspar and rock fragments.

Soil texture is described by the relative proportions of sand, silt, and clay, plotted on the U.S. Department of Agriculture soil texture diagram; the sand and silt components are dominated by quartz, while the clay component is dominated by clay minerals.

Soil forms through the accumulation and decay of organic matter and through mechanical and chemical weathering; it forms most readily under temperate to tropical conditions with moderate precipitation, because warmth speeds chemical and biochemical reactions and enhances plant growth; too much water leaches important chemical nutrients and produces acidic soils, while too little water limits downward transport and leads to the accumulation of salts and carbonate minerals from upward-moving water.

Parent material can be bedrock or any unconsolidated sediment (such as glacial or stream deposits); quartz-rich parent material such as granite, sandstone, or loose sand leads to sandy soils, while basaltic parent material generates fertile soils providing phosphorus, iron, magnesium, and calcium; clay minerals have large surface areas with negative charges attractive to positively charged nutrient elements such as calcium, magnesium, iron, and potassium.

Soil can only develop where surface materials remain in place; soils cannot develop where the rate of soil formation is less than the rate of erosion, so steep slopes tend to have little or no soil, and even under ideal conditions soil takes thousands of years to develop.

Soil development generally involves the downward movement of clay, water, and dissolved ions, producing chemically and texturally distinct layers called soil horizons: O is the layer of organic matter; A is partially decayed organic matter mixed with mineral material; E is the eluviated (leached) layer from which clay and iron have been removed, leaving a pale layer that may be sandier; B is the layer of accumulation of clay, iron, and other elements from the overlying soil; C is the layer of incomplete weathering.

Under natural conditions on gentle slopes, the rate of soil formation either balances or exceeds the rate of erosion; human practices related to forestry and agriculture have significantly upset this balance, and soils are held in place by vegetation, so when vegetation is removed the protection is temporarily or permanently lost.

The Food and Agriculture Organization defines soil degradation as a change in the soil health status resulting in a diminished capacity of the ecosystem to provide goods and services for its beneficiaries; soil erosion refers to absolute soil losses in terms of topsoil and nutrients, is the most visible effect of soil degradation, is a natural process in mountainous areas, and is often made much worse by poor management practices.

Soil is one of Earth's carbon reservoirs: most of Earth's carbon is stored in rocks, and the rest is in the ocean, atmosphere, plants, soil, and fossil fuels; exposing soil through land-use change can vent carbon from decayed plant matter into the atmosphere.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The two main sources list different numbers of soil-forming factors.
positions: USDA NRCS (Soil Taxonomy): five factors — climate (including water and temperature effects), macro- and microorganisms, conditioned by relief, acting on parent material over time.

Open Textbook BC Physical Geology 5.4: climate (especially average temperature and precipitation and the consequent vegetation), the type of parent material, the slope of the surface, and the amount of time available — organisms appear through vegetation and biological activity rather than as a separate listed factor.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the five-factor framework from the official NRCS/Soil Taxonomy definition and folds the Open Textbook's vegetation and biological detail into the climate and organisms factors; both sources agree on the same underlying set of controls.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Soil composition percentages differ across sources and contexts.
positions: Open Textbook BC Physical Geology 5.4: approximately 45 percent minerals, 5 percent organic matter, 50 percent pore space filled with air and water.
Other sources give different splits depending on soil type and depth (not verified in this research pass).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Only the Open Textbook BC figures are used, stated as approximate, with the arithmetic check 45 + 5 + 50 = 100 percent; no other composition claims were made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Terminology for soils developed on transported material.
positions: The term 'transported soil' is commonly used for soils on transported material such as glacial sediments.
Open Textbook BC Physical Geology 5.4 notes this term is misleading because the soil itself has not been transported, and recommends 'soil developed on unconsolidated material.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids 'transported soil' and uses the recommended phrasing 'soil on unconsolidated material' for the contrast entry.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft in public/content/phase-3/lessons.json for earth-and-space-science:foundations:soil contained only generic boilerplate with no domain content: 'Soil is a foundational concept in Earth & Space Science. This lesson introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it.', 'College courses use soil as a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions.', 'Think of soil as a label on a toolbox drawer.', and 'Like reading a map legend before choosing a route.' None of these were supported by research; all were discarded and replaced with source-verified content.
correctionsNeeded: Compaction as a degradation mechanism was cut: the FAO soil-degradation sub-pages for salinization and compaction returned 404 and had no Wayback captures, and no other accessible authoritative source was found, so no compaction claims are published.

Salinization was limited to the verified mechanism: Open Textbook BC 5.4 states that in dry regions with too little water, salts and carbonate minerals accumulate from upward-moving water. Irrigation-driven salinization was not verifiable and was cut.

Soil erosion is framed strictly as a degradation form (loss of topsoil and nutrients; natural on mountainsides; worsened by poor management; vegetation holds soil in place), with transport mechanics deliberately deferred to the sibling erosion topic.
All numeric claims were checked arithmetically: 45 percent minerals + 5 percent organic matter + 50 percent pore space = 100 percent; sand/silt/clay are the only texture classes used.
The USDA texture diagram claim was softened to what the source states (a diagram of relative proportions of sand, silt, and clay) without enumerating textural class names not verified in the capture.
Earth's carbon reservoir claim is attributed to NASA Earth Observatory, which lists soil among the reservoirs (rocks, ocean, atmosphere, plants, soil, fossil fuels).

Supports the Soil Taxonomy (second edition) definition of soil as a natural body comprised of solids (minerals and organic matter), liquid, and gases, characterized by horizons/layers or by the ability to support rooted plants, with the classification lower boundary at 200 cm; the five soil-forming factors — climate (including water and temperature effects), macro- and microorganisms, conditioned by relief, acting on parent material over a period of time; and the Soil Science Society of America statement that soils perform vital functions to sustain plant and animal life, regulate water flow, filter and buffer pollutants, cycle nutrients, and provide physical stability and support.
